tagline.text: An island of green hills and surf, shaped by Pacific winds

items.credit: L. from Rotherham, Yorkshire, United Kingdom / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons
National Historical Commission of the Philippines / Public domain / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The "Land of the Howling Winds," facing the Pacific head-on off the east coast of the Bicol mainland. From Binurong Point, where green hills drop into cliffs, to Puraran Beach with its legendary Majestic wave, to the coral-stone Bato Church and waterfalls, this is a raw island landscape with few tourists.

Catanduanes is a province made up of a single island of about 1,500 sq km, sitting off the coast of Tabaco in Albay province, at the southeastern tip of Luzon. Its east coast opens directly onto the Pacific, so it's often the first place typhoons entering the Philippines pass through, earning it the nickname "Land of the Howling Winds." The capital is Virac on the south coast, home to the airport, port, and most commerce.

Most of the island is dense mountain forest, and the abaca (Manila hemp) grown here accounts for more than a third of the Philippines' total production, earning Catanduanes the title "Abaca Capital." The coast alternates between black rock cliffs carved by rough seas and green grassy hills, with Binurong Point — nicknamed "Little Batanes" for its resemblance to Batanes — as the signature view. Sites across the island trace its history too, like Bato Church, built of coral stone during the Spanish era, and Luyang Cave, where residents are said to have hidden from Moro raiders.

To surfers, Catanduanes is famous for a wave called "Majestic." It breaks hard to the right over the coral reef in front of Puraran Beach in Baras town, growing biggest while a typhoon lingers out in the Pacific, and it has drawn surfers from abroad for years. In months with no swell, the same beach turns into a calm coral lagoon, good for snorkeling and relaxing.

With almost no resort developments or large hotels, and few tourists, this island suits travelers worn out by the crowds of Boracay or El Nido. On the other hand, public transport is scarce and the weather is unpredictable, so it's best recommended to travelers who enjoy renting a motorbike or van to get around independently and building slack into their schedule.
From Ginsaanan village in Baras, a
30–40 minute
walk through forest trail and grassy hills opens onto green cliffs dropping to the Pacific. Climb up in time for sunrise and the hills turn gold.

blocks.title: Puraran Beach and the Majestic wave

children.text: A beach with a wave that's legendary among Filipino surfers. Beginners can take a lesson from a local instructor on smaller-wave days, and on calm days, the inside of the reef is great for snorkeling.
Another viewpoint hill on the Baras coast near Binurong Point, with a gazebo and a walking path, good for a quick stop to look out over the Pacific and the coastline.
Built of coral stone by residents over more than 50 years, from
to
, this Church of St. John the Baptist is one of the island's oldest stone churches.
A tiered waterfall close to Virac town, with a wide pool for swimming that makes it a favorite weekend spot for local families. Admission is cheap and access is easy.
From Sacahon Beach in Bato, a
30–45 minute
climb reaches the hilltop lighthouse. On clear days, you can see Mayon Volcano across the water.
A crescent-shaped beach in Igang village, Virac, marked by two rock islets rising offshore. Resort facilities and a water slide make it convenient for family trips.

Luyang Cave in San Andres carries the tragic story of residents who hid there to escape pirates, while Nahulugan Falls in Gigmoto to the east is a three-tier waterfall in the forest, a good destination for an around-the-island drive.

Catanduanes has no clearly defined dry season and sees rain year-round. Within that,
March–June
, with the least rain and calmest seas, is the best time for trekking and beach trips. Midday temperatures during this period run around
, and the grassy hills at Binurong Point stay a deep green.
Surf season runs
August–October

. Swells generated by typhoons lingering out in the Pacific reach Puraran and make the Majestic wave biggest, but for the same reason, the risk of a typhoon passing directly over the island is high too. In fact, Typhoon Goni (Rolly) in 2020 and Typhoon Man-yi (Pepito) in 2024 both made landfall on this island and caused major damage.
November–January
overlaps with the northeast monsoon Amihan and brings the heaviest rain and frequent boat cancellations, so first-time visitors are better off avoiding it.

For a first visit, it's convenient to base yourself in Virac, where the airport, terminal, and restaurants are concentrated, and tour the island on day trips. Hotels and pensions in town run about

a night, while the resorts at Twin Rock Beach in Igang, west of town, offer both beach and pool access, popular with families. If surfing or the Binurong sunrise is your goal, the simple surfer accommodations at Puraran Beach are the better choice — a fan room runs about
a night, with the long-running Majestic Puraran Beach Resort a well-known option. Beach accommodations can have unreliable power and internet.

The food here centers on Bicolano cuisine. Laing (taro leaves simmered in coconut milk), Bicol Express (stir-fried in coconut milk with hot chilies), and kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar) are available almost everywhere. Named for Bato town, pancit Bato — sun-dried rice noodles stir-fried — is the island's specialty, available for about
a plate at market snack stalls. Tuna, lobster, and crab caught in the Pacific are fresh and cheap too, and a meal at a simple restaurant runs about
. Bags and hats woven from abaca fiber make good souvenirs.
ATMs exist essentially only in Virac. Bring plenty of cash for admission fees and lodging before heading to Baras or Puraran.

Register at the village tourism office to climb Binurong Point with an assigned guide; the guide fee is per team of 1–4 people, so it's cheaper if you're splitting it with a group. Rates and rules can change, so check the on-site notice.
To catch the sunrise, you'll need to leave Virac around
4 AM
, so it's best to arrange a time with your motorbike or tricycle driver the night before.

The round-island road is mostly paved now, but the east coast has long, winding mountain stretches that get slippery in the rain. If you're not confident riding a motorbike, a chartered van with a driver is the safer option.
Beginner surfers shouldn't go into Majestic on big-wave days — practice instead at the inner point a local instructor picks out.
If you're traveling by boat, don't book a return flight or bus for the same afternoon — leave at least half a day of buffer for safety.
Smart and Globe signals reach Virac and major villages, but drop out on the eastern mountain roads and coastal cliff stretches. Download offline maps in advance.

Catanduanes is one of the places in the Philippines typhoons cross most often. During the rainy and typhoon season, check PAGASA forecasts and coast guard departure notices daily, and don't hesitate to postpone your plans if a warning is issued.
The cliff edge at Binurong Point has no railing and strong wind. Don't get too close to the edge for photos, and wear trekking shoes since the grass trail turns slippery after rain.
Puraran and the east coast take Pacific swells directly, with strong rip currents. Don't swim out past the reef.
The reef exposed at low tide is sharp and has plenty of sea urchins, so aqua shoes are needed.
Remote villages are far from hospitals and pharmacies, so bring basic medicine and insect repellent.
Mountain roads have almost no streetlights, making driving after dark dangerous — plan to reach your accommodation before nightfall.
